Near midnight, because she could not go home and could not sign and could not stand to sit doing neither, Wren took the ledgers out of the bottom drawer again. All eleven of them. She stacked them on the desk in order, 1946 to 1987, and she opened the oldest one, and she began to read.

Not the columns that added up. The margins.

She had seen the hook-shaped mark before, the curl like a wave, beside the Pell loans. Now she saw that it was everywhere. It was beside an entry from 1951: *Crossing, Okafor family, 4 pers., furniture.* No fare recorded. A hook. It was beside an entry from 1963: *Night run, Dr. Lee to island, Pruitt baby.* No fare. A hook. It was beside an entry from 1972: *Gunderson, fuel advance, $300, boat repairs after storm.* Never repaid. A hook.

Wren turned the pages faster.

There were hundreds of them. Thousands, maybe. Forty years of crossings with no fare, of fuel lent and never returned, of bags of groceries carried for free to the island in the hard winter of 1978, of medical runs in the middle of the night, of a wedding in 1969 when the bride's family couldn't pay and her father had written *gift* in the fare column and then crossed it out and drawn a hook. Every one of them in his small upright hand. Every one marked.

He hadn't been bad with money. He'd been keeping a different set of books.

*A ledger only tells you what was paid. It never tells you what was owed.*

On a page from 1977 she found it. *T. Halloway, $4,000.* No date of repayment. Beside it, not a hook. Something else. Two words, in pencil, pressed so lightly they were almost gone: *forgiven, always.*

She was still sitting with her finger on those words when Ada knocked on the window. The harbor master was in her nightgown under her coat, and her white hair was loose, and she had a flashlight.

"I saw the lamp from the tower," Ada said, when Wren let her in. "Again." She looked at the ledgers stacked across the desk, open, their margins crawling with small curled marks. Her face changed. "Ah. You found them."

"You knew."

"Everybody knew a little. Nobody knew all of it, except him." Ada sat down heavily on the passenger bench. "Elias never sent anyone a bill in his life, Wren. Not for the hard things. He just carried them. Half this town owes your family something. Some of them owe you their lives. Marguerite Okafor's mother came across this sound in your grandfather's skiff in 1951 with three children and everything they owned, and they didn't have a nickel, and your grandfather wrote it down and never asked."

Wren looked at the pages. "He never collected."

"He didn't need to, while he was alive. People just knew." Ada nodded at the stack. "He was saving it, I think. In case. In case there was ever a day when the family needed the town the way the town had needed the family."

"Why didn't he use it? When Pell came. Why borrow?"

"Pride," Ada said simply. "The same reason your brother didn't come to the funeral. The Halloway men would rather drown than ask."

The word *drown* lay between them. Wren closed the 1977 ledger with her finger still inside it, marking the place.

"I'm not a Halloway man," she said.

Ada looked at her for a long moment, and then the old woman smiled, slow and fierce, the first real smile Wren had seen on her since March.

"No," Ada said. "You're the bookkeeper."

Wren pulled a fresh legal pad toward her and uncapped her own pen, the cheap blue one, not Corwin Pell's. At the top of the page she wrote: *Accounts receivable.* Then she opened the 1951 ledger and started copying out names.
